subject: zoology
question_text: Give an account of flow of energy in an ecosystem.

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya Junior Fastrack zoology section (book p.27, LAQ 11). Zoology holds only ONE source book — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only, and no zoology board paper is in the corpus — so the two-book union check and the back-test are both structurally impossible for this card; 'not checked' does NOT mean 'checked and clean'. The mark split is a claim until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

steps.label: Source of energy and PAR
lines: The sun is the only source of energy for all
the ecosystems on the earth.
The solar energy captured by plants passes
through the different organisms of an
ecosystem.
Less than 50% of the incident solar energy
is Photosynthetically Active Radiation
(PAR).
Plants capture only 2 to 10% of PAR, and
this sustains the entire living world.
All heterotrophs depend on the producers for
their food, either directly or indirectly.
steps.why: Energy flow is a one-way street from the sun, so the answer starts at the sun and follows the energy down through two losses — the part of sunlight that is not PAR, and the part of PAR the plant cannot capture.
common_mistakes: Writing that plants capture 2 to 10% of sunlight. It is 2 to 10% of PAR, not of all sunlight.
Calling the sun the main source. In this answer it is the ONLY source.
steps.memory_tip: Two cuts before the food chain even starts: under half of sunlight is PAR, and only 2 to 10% of that is captured.
steps.margin_note: Both percentages with the quantity each belongs to. Five short statements.

steps.label: Diagram — energy flow

elements.caption: Step 1 — the four tiers of the pyramid
Step 2 — the energy stored at each level
Step 3 — the 10% arrows going up the pyramid
Step 5 — the names of the trophic levels

steps.why: Energy flow is a quantity that shrinks at every step, so the picture that carries it is a stack of tiers that narrow upwards; drawing it to scale makes the 10% law visible instead of merely stated.
common_mistakes: Drawing the tiers the same width. Each level must be visibly smaller than the one below it.
Putting the producers at the top. The producers are the widest tier at the BOTTOM.
Leaving the energy values off. The numbers 100, 10 and 1 kJ are what show the 10% law.
steps.memory_tip: Draw the widest tier at the bottom first, then stack narrower ones on it. Write the energy inside each tier.
steps.margin_note: Label the trophic levels and write the energy in each tier. The 10% arrows carry the marks.

steps.label: First law of thermodynamics
lines: The first law of thermodynamics is the law
of conservation of energy.
It states that energy is neither created nor
destroyed. It may change from one form to
another.
The energy that reaches the earth is
balanced by the energy that leaves it as
heat radiation.
Transfer of energy is essential for the
survival of life, and it needs a continuous
flow of energy.
steps.why: The first law explains why energy has to keep arriving: none of it is lost from the universe, but it changes into forms an organism cannot use, so the supply must be continuous.
common_mistakes: Writing that energy is destroyed at each level. It is not destroyed; it CHANGES FORM.
Leaving out the balance between energy arriving and heat leaving.
steps.memory_tip: First law says nothing is lost; second law says what is left is not always usable.
steps.margin_note: State the law, then the balance, then why the flow must be continuous.

steps.label: Second law and energy flow
lines: The second law of thermodynamics states that
there is degradation of energy at each
level.
The degraded energy is in the form of
unavailable heat energy.
It constitutes entropy, that is, energy that
is not available for work.
The transfer of energy through a food chain
is known as energy flow.
The amount of energy available decreases at
successive trophic levels.
When an organism dies, it becomes a source
of energy for its decomposers.
steps.why: This step defines energy flow itself and gives the reason it runs one way only: at every transfer some energy is degraded to heat, so less is available at each level up.
common_mistakes: Writing that entropy is heat. Entropy is the energy that is NOT AVAILABLE for work.
Writing that energy increases up the chain. It DECREASES at successive trophic levels.
Leaving out the decomposers. Dead organisms pass their energy on to them.
steps.memory_tip: At every step some energy turns into heat that no organism can use. That is why the chain is short.
steps.margin_note: Two marks, so keep all six points. Define energy flow in the middle of them.

steps.label: Standing crop
lines: Each trophic level has a certain mass of
living material, and this is called the
standing crop.
The standing crop is the biomass of that
level.
Biomass can be expressed in terms of fresh
weight or dry weight.
Dry weight is more accurate, because the
water content of a body varies.
steps.why: Energy at a trophic level is measured through the mass of living material there, so the standing crop is the bridge between the energy account and something that can actually be weighed.
common_mistakes: Calling the standing crop the number of organisms. It is their MASS.
Writing that fresh weight is more accurate. DRY weight is the accurate measure.
steps.memory_tip: Standing crop is what is standing there now, weighed. Dry weight, because water is not food.
steps.margin_note: Define it, name it as biomass, then the two weights with dry weight preferred.

steps.label: The 10% law

lines.text: Only 10% passes up; 90% is spent as heat

lines: The 10% law was introduced by Lindeman.
During the transfer of energy, only 10% of
the energy is stored in the next trophic
level. The rest is used for metabolic
activities such as respiration.
Lindeman's 10% rule is the most widely used
measure of ecological efficiency.
Ex: if the net primary production of the
plants is 100 kJ, the biomass available to
the herbivores is 10 kJ, and the next
carnivores get only 1 kJ.
steps.why: The 10% law puts a number on everything said above, and the worked example with 100, 10 and 1 kJ is what proves the loss at each step rather than just asserting it.
common_mistakes: Writing that 10% is lost. Ten per cent is what is PASSED ON; ninety per cent is used up.
Leaving out Lindeman's name, which the question paper looks for.
Giving the law without the worked numbers.
steps.memory_tip: 100, 10, 1 — drop a zero at every trophic level.
steps.margin_note: Name Lindeman, state the law, then the three numbers. Close the answer here.

insider_note: Two things are checked by name in this answer: Lindeman for the 10% law, and the worked example of 100 kJ, 10 kJ and 1 kJ.
